purpose: Source-checked original paraphrases of accessible full articles. Each entry identifies the source and review scope.

articles.title: Prompt-based emotional scaffolding in generative AI: Effects on self-regulated learning and socio-emotional outcomes
articles.license_context: Publisher open-access article; Crossref/OpenAlex record reports CC BY-NC-ND. Only newly written factual paraphrases are recorded, not article text or adapted figures.
articles.method: A preregistered randomized classroom experiment assigned 144 Danish high-school students to standard ChatGPT, an AI chatbot that guided self-regulated learning (SRLbot), or the same approach with emotional support (Emotional SRLbot), with 48 participants in each condition. One learning session lasted about 25 minutes. Tests and surveys were administered before and after, and 85 students completed a four-week follow-up. Interaction traces were coded to examine self-regulatory behaviors.
articles.results: All three groups improved on immediate conceptual-knowledge and learning-transfer tests; however, condition-by-time comparisons were not statistically significant for either outcome (p = .980 and p = .953). At the four-week follow-up, knowledge and transfer change likewise did not differ significantly between groups. Both SRL-based chatbot groups showed larger improvements in enjoyment and reductions in boredom than the general-purpose ChatGPT group. Emotional SRLbot also showed higher task-level performance and reflection indicators in the interaction traces. Hopelessness fell across all groups without a differential treatment effect, and self-efficacy and chatbot trust did not show clear between-group benefits.
articles.discussion: The authors interpret the findings as preliminary support for combining AI prompts about planning, monitoring and reflection with encouragement sensitive to students' emotional states. An intervention that makes learning feel better and increases momentary self-regulatory behavior is not yet evidence of lasting independent learning gains. Theoretical expectations about emotional regulation pathways were not themselves fully tested as causal mediators.
articles.limitations: The intervention lasted only one 25-minute session. The pretest and follow-up knowledge measures had internal consistency below .60, making the learning estimates less reliable. Only 85 of the original 144 returned for follow-up, and dropout related to prior AI experience and initial boredom. Some self-report and trace-based measures diverged, and trace coding was aggregated across each session rather than modeling the sequence of regulatory behaviors. Several outcome comparisons were tested and longer-term effects remain uncertain.

digest.idea: Emotionally responsive AI improved some learning experiences, not measured learning gains over ChatGPT.
digest.explain: In a randomized high-school trial, adding self-regulation prompts and emotional support changed how students felt and engaged during the task, but did not establish superior knowledge or transfer gains.
digest.approach: Preregistered three-arm classroom experiment (144 students; 48 per condition) comparing ChatGPT, an SRL-supporting chatbot and an emotionally supportive SRL chatbot; 85 completed a four-week follow-up.
digest.finding: Tailored agents increased enjoyment and reduced boredom relative to ChatGPT; emotional scaffolding also strengthened observed task-level regulation. Immediate learning gains occurred in all groups, without a statistically significant advantage for the tailored agents.
digest.interpretation: The promise is improved support for moment-to-moment self-regulated work, rather than proof that emotionally responsive AI builds durable independent thinking.
digest.limitation: A single 25-minute intervention, attrition at follow-up, and weak reliability in some knowledge tests limit the learning and retention claims.

articles.review_scope: Original Wiley HTML article, including study methods, results tables and reported limitations; paraphrase and synthesis checked against source. Not an independently replicated analysis.

articles.title: Cognitive Predictors of AI-Related Textual Change in Upper-Intermediate L2 Russian Writing: Working Memory, Attention Control, and Critical Thinking
articles.license_context: Open publisher HTML reviewed. This record contains original factual paraphrases only.
articles.review_scope: Sections 3.3–3.6, 4.2–4.4 and 5.6; Tables 3–5.
articles.method: Thirty-eight upper-intermediate learners each wrote twice about a hobby, a month apart. AI access order was counterbalanced. Researchers compared eleven text measures and examined associations with premeasured cognitive abilities.
articles.results: The AI-assisted texts contained longer words, more connectives and fewer first-person markers. Stronger attention control was associated with a smaller increase in one vocabulary-diversity measure across sensitivity checks.
articles.discussion: The authors interpret the differences as changes in the final texts. They could not trace which suggestions writers accepted or show that their unassisted language skills improved.
articles.limitations: One prompt per condition, a small sample, and many unadjusted tests make the individual-difference results exploratory.

digest.idea: AI-assisted Russian essays used longer words and fewer first-person expressions
digest.explain: The study compared what writers produced with and without AI, including how their vocabulary changed.
digest.approach: Two timed compositions per learner, with and without AI.
digest.finding: When AI was available, writers used longer words and more connectives. Total word count showed no clear difference.
digest.interpretation: Changes in the finished text do not establish independent language learning.
digest.limitation: Thirty-eight writers answered the same prompt twice. The study tested many associations.

articles.title: Cognitive-Professional Resource Configurations for AI-Mediated Teaching: Perceived Teacher-Education Support and Intelligent Professional Action
articles.license_context: Open publisher HTML reviewed. This record contains original factual paraphrases only.
articles.review_scope: Methods 3.1–3.4, Results 4.3–4.6 and Discussion 5.4–5.5; Tables 7–10.
articles.method: At one Chinese university, researchers surveyed trainee teachers in a national preparation program. A profile analysis grouped 942 responses using ratings of digital literacy, resilience, judgment about AI-generated knowledge and AI-related teaching knowledge.
articles.results: Four profiles mainly differed in overall self-rated resources. Reported teaching innovation competence rose across those groups. More perceived support was associated with higher-resource profiles.
articles.discussion: The authors suggest checking whether the survey patterns appear in lesson design and observed teaching.
articles.limitations: The measures were collected together at one institution. Respondents rated their own capabilities, and alternate screening decisions changed the profile composition.

digest.idea: Trainee teachers who felt better supported also felt more prepared to innovate
digest.explain: The survey compared educators’ perceptions of their training, their digital skills and their readiness to change teaching practice.
digest.approach: Cross-sectional survey and profile analysis of 942 trainee teachers.
digest.finding: People in higher-resource profiles also gave themselves higher ratings for teaching innovation.
digest.interpretation: The profiles describe perceived readiness for AI-mediated teaching.
digest.limitation: Observed classroom performance and training effects were not measured.

articles.title: From Gradual Release of Responsibility to Gradual Release of Technology: A Case for the Staged Use of AI in Formal Education
articles.license_context: Open publisher HTML reviewed. This record contains original factual paraphrases only.
articles.review_scope: Sections 2–4, especially Figure 1 and stages 4.1–4.3, and closing implications.
articles.method: The author draws on selected learning-science literature on practice, memory, cognitive effort and judging one’s knowledge to adapt the gradual-release model.
articles.results: The paper presents a framework without collecting new outcome data.
articles.discussion: Progression depends on the skill and learning goal. A student ready to delegate a familiar step may still need independent practice on an unfamiliar one.
articles.limitations: The review is selective and does not test the proposed stages against other teaching approaches.

digest.idea: Let the skill a student can demonstrate guide when to introduce AI
digest.explain: The proposed model gives teachers a way to decide when students should work independently, share the task with AI or delegate a step.
digest.approach: Conceptual synthesis and a three-stage instructional proposal.
digest.interpretation: Begin with independent practice, introduce constrained assistance, then allow selective delegation after the learner shows mastery.
digest.limitation: The model’s proposed progression still needs classroom testing.

articles.title: Augmentation or Erosion? Regulating Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Supported STEM Learning
articles.license_context: Open publisher HTML reviewed. This record contains original factual paraphrases only.
articles.review_scope: Full theory article, especially The Central Principle, A Research Program for Developing Offloading Regulation, and Limitations and Scope.
articles.method: The author integrates research on cognitive offloading, distributed cognition, cognitive load and self-regulation to develop predictions for STEM learning.
articles.results: This article proposes an explanation and tests for future studies. It reports no new experiment.
articles.discussion: Students may use AI for peripheral operations while retaining or later reconstructing the reasoning they need to learn. The author proposes checking AI output against discipline-specific evidence.
articles.limitations: The proposed regulatory capacities still need measurement and tests distinguishing them from subject knowledge and general self-regulation.

digest.idea: What students delegate matters for what they learn
digest.explain: A step that can be delegated in one lesson may be the very skill another lesson asks a student to develop.
digest.approach: Theory development using literature and worked disciplinary examples.
digest.interpretation: Identify which reasoning serves the learning goal. Check machine-produced work against the subject’s standards and practice reconstructing essential steps.
digest.limitation: The framework’s predictions and measures remain untested.

articles.title: Trust in Generative AI and Critical Thinking Among College Students: A Structural Equation Modeling Analysis Based on Perceived Usefulness, Cognitive Offloading, and AI Self-Efficacy
articles.license_context: The linked publisher or university copy was readable. Only original factual paraphrases are included.
articles.method: Cheng and Li analyzed questionnaires from 976 students at three colleges in China. They modeled how trust, perceived usefulness, confidence using AI and delegation related to students’ accounts of how they evaluate information.
articles.results: Trust was positively associated with reported critical thinking. Perceived usefulness and confidence showed positive indirect associations, while greater reported delegation showed a negative indirect association.
articles.discussion: Students who trusted AI also described judgments and habits with different relationships to thinking critically. A trust score alone obscures that distinction.
articles.limitations: The convenience sample completed all measures once. The model cannot show which came first or whether students performed better on a critical-thinking task.

articles.title: Knowing (Not) to Know: Explainable Artificial Intelligence and Human Metacognition
articles.license_context: The linked publisher or university copy was readable. Only original factual paraphrases are included.
articles.method: Von Zahn and colleagues tested whether seeing how an algorithm weights features changes which cases people delegate. One experiment asked 149 German real estate agents to price apartments. The other used loan-repayment predictions.
articles.results: Among the agents, exposure to explanations reduced average overconfidence from 43.3 to 29.3 percentage points. Delegation rose from 41% to 54%. The change in confidence did not coincide with a statistically detectable improvement in unaided pricing accuracy.
articles.discussion: The explanation provided information about the model and gave participants a reason to reconsider their own judgment before assigning work.
articles.limitations: Participants decided who would take a case before seeing the AI prediction. They received no performance feedback between delegation choices. Results may differ when people learn over repeated exchanges or can revise an assignment.

articles.title: Disrupted network reconfiguration during task switching in insomnia: the role of sleep-related attentional bias
articles.license_context: The linked publisher or university copy was readable. Only original factual paraphrases are included.
articles.method: Yang and colleagues compared 24 adults with insomnia and 24 controls using questionnaires and a task-switching experiment during functional MRI. Trials used general images and images related to sleep.
articles.results: The insomnia group reported lower cognitive flexibility and responded faster overall. The groups did not differ significantly in the extra response time or loss of accuracy when a rule changed. Several patterns of brain activity or connectivity differed between groups.
articles.discussion: Participants’ experience, measured speed and brain activity describe different aspects of task switching. The behavioral contrasts did not establish a specific attentional bias toward sleep-related images.
articles.limitations: This small cross-sectional study cannot establish why the groups differed. A fixed block order may have affected results. The study did not involve AI.

articles.title: Cognitive offloading in student–AI collaboration: A longitudinal analysis of prompting strategies
articles.license_context: The public copy names an article author as uploader and includes the publisher imprint and CC BY 4.0 license. The Observatory provides original factual paraphrases.
articles.method: Misiejuk and colleagues coded 281 AI prompts across 122 submissions on four assignments in a social network analysis course. They compared how prompt features occurred together in higher- and lower-quality work.
articles.results: Higher-quality submissions more often paired instructions with background details. Lower-quality submissions more often contained disagreement or commands with little context.
articles.discussion: The prompts give a record of what students asked AI to do. Providing context can look different from repeatedly telling the tool that its output is wrong.
articles.limitations: The task required structured datasets. Prompt wording was a proxy for thinking, and the design cannot show that one wording strategy produced better learning or reduced mental effort.

articles.title: Investigating students’ cognitive processes in generative AI-assisted digital multimodal composing and traditional writing
articles.license_context: The public copy names an article author as uploader and includes the publisher imprint and CC BY 4.0 license. The Observatory provides original factual paraphrases.
articles.method: Liu and colleagues followed eight Chinese undergraduate volunteers at a New Zealand university for two weeks. Four wrote an essay and four made slides on the same topic. Screen recordings, think-aloud accounts, completed work and interviews documented their choices.
articles.results: Slide makers used AI to find examples and connect claims. Some took a proposed image description from one tool to another, then reviewed and revised the image for the slide.
articles.discussion: Making a slide deck gave students decisions about the relationship between an image and its argument that an essay did not require in the same way.
articles.limitations: Eight volunteers at a single university completed different assignments. The qualitative evidence describes strategies and does not establish an improvement in writing ability or attention.

articles.title: Layer-sensitive cognitive offloading in generative AI-assisted writing: supported performance and independent no-AI outcomes
articles.license_context: The publisher provides an open-access article. These notes contain original paraphrases only.
articles.method: Six university English-writing classes in China followed one of three approaches for eight weeks. Students wrote without AI, chose how to use AI, or followed limits on what they could delegate and explained their choices. The analysis included 168 students. Everyone completed a supervised writing and revision task without AI at the end.
articles.results: Students who chose freely how to use AI had the highest observed writing scores during supported work. Students with delegation limits and required reflection had the highest observed scores on all four final unaided outcomes, including argument depth and revision quality. Open collaboration also involved more delegation of ideas and reasoning. Estimates accounting for the six classes were imprecise.
articles.discussion: The authors distinguish the quality of writing a student can produce with help from the choices the student can make independently on another piece in the same genre.
articles.limitations: Whole classes followed different approaches, so class differences could affect the comparison. The study cannot separate the effects of reflection and delegation limits, and it measured no delayed or cross-genre transfer.

digest.idea: Who wrote best changed when the AI was taken away
digest.explain: Students with broad access produced the highest-scoring assisted drafts. Their classmates who had to explain and limit AI use led on the unaided assessment.
digest.approach: Researchers followed 168 students across six English-writing classes and scored a final supervised task.
digest.finding: The bounded-support group had the highest observed unaided writing quality, higher-order thinking, argument-depth and revision scores. Open collaboration led during assisted writing.
digest.interpretation: A polished assisted draft and an independently revised essay measure different things.
digest.limitation: Six intact classes shared three conditions. Class differences, limits on delegation and required reflection cannot be disentangled.

articles.title: Perceived and demonstrated generative AI literacy in engineering problem solving: the role of verification behavior
articles.license_context: The publisher provides an open-access article. These notes contain original paraphrases only.
articles.method: At three Chinese universities, 1,206 engineering undergraduates rated their AI literacy, completed a scenario test, and reported how often they checked AI output. Two scored engineering problems required them to spot and correct flawed advice on shaft stresses and material selection.
articles.results: Self-rated literacy and scenario-test performance correlated at r = .265, sharing about 7% of their variance. Higher scenario scores were associated with more frequent reported checks after adjustment. More checking was also associated with better engineering answers. The authors found an indirect association in both their proposed ordering and a reversed ordering.
articles.discussion: The authors treat confidence, tested literacy and checking habits as different aspects of AI use. Students' descriptions of checking can complement task evidence, but neither alone establishes what was verified correctly.
articles.limitations: The online assessments were unproctored, so independent performance could not be confirmed. The survey measured reported checking frequency, not the quality of the checks. The single-time-point design cannot establish causal direction.

digest.idea: Confidence in AI literacy only modestly tracked tested skill
digest.explain: Students could rate themselves highly without scoring equally highly on scenarios that required them to evaluate AI output.
digest.approach: 1,206 engineering students completed an online questionnaire, a literacy test and two tasks with flawed AI advice.
digest.finding: Self-ratings and tested literacy shared about 7% of their variance. Higher test scores accompanied more reported checking, which in turn was associated with better engineering answers.
digest.interpretation: A confidence rating cannot substitute for testing how students handle a plausible but flawed answer.
digest.limitation: Checking was self-reported and the assessment was unproctored. The associations do not establish the order of effects.

articles.title: Between cognitive offloading and critical autonomy: a systematic review of the epistemic implications of generative AI in higher education
articles.license_context: The publisher provides an open-access article. These notes contain original paraphrases only.
articles.method: Reviewers searched Scopus, Web of Science and databases available through EBSCOhost. They coded findings from 26 eligible higher-education studies and compared themes across different study designs.
articles.results: One recurring theme concerned checking whether plausible AI output was reliable. The included studies described incorrect answers and fabricated citations, alongside verification practices such as comparing other sources. The review organized these observations thematically and did not estimate a pooled change in students' reasoning.
articles.discussion: The authors propose teaching students to evaluate the support behind AI answers and to explain who is responsible for a claim. They present their framework as a provisional interpretation of the included studies.
articles.limitations: The search excluded grey literature. Differences in design, populations and measures constrained comparison, and the proposed framework has not been independently validated.

digest.idea: Plausible answers make verification a separate learning task
digest.explain: A review of higher-education research traces how students decide whether to trust AI-generated claims and citations.
digest.approach: Reviewers coded findings from 26 studies of generative AI in higher education.
digest.finding: Checking sources recurred across studies. Individual accounts described students encountering convincing errors and false citations, as well as efforts to cross-check them.
digest.interpretation: The authors propose making evaluation of AI-produced evidence an explicit part of coursework.
digest.limitation: The studies used different designs. Their patterns do not establish how often students check AI or the effect of a specific intervention.

articles.title: Beyond the tool: a systematic realist synthesis of cognitive agency in human-GenAI interaction in higher education
articles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
articles.license_context: Publisher open access. The notes paraphrase the article.
articles.method: Researchers coded 93 higher-education studies for the work students delegated, their responses to AI output and evidence of learning without assistance. They distinguished reported behavior from inferences based on the assignment design.
articles.results: Eighty-five studies identified delegated tasks, 44 described how students responded to AI and 24 measured learning without AI. Only four documented both responses and independent learning. One learner rejected a suggestion that conflicted with the terminology in their own text.
articles.discussion: The authors propose recording when students question or revise an answer and pairing that record with an independent task. Together those measures can connect a decision during practice to what the student can later do.
articles.limitations: Half of the 44 studies describing responses relied on self-reports or author summaries. Follow-up was too short to assess cumulative effects.

digest.idea: Who checked the AI answer?
digest.explain: A review tracked which steps in AI-assisted learning researchers could actually see.
digest.approach: Reviewers asked what work students handed to AI in 93 higher-education studies. They also looked for evidence of what students did with its answer and what they could do later without AI.
digest.finding: Eighty-five studies identified a task students handed to AI. Only four documented both how students handled its answer and how they performed without it.
digest.interpretation: Tracking a student's correction can reveal work a finished assignment conceals.
digest.limitation: Of the 44 studies describing a response to AI, 22 relied on students’ recollections or the researchers’ account. Longer-term changes in independent reasoning remain unknown.

articles.title: Motivational gain trumps cognitive offloading: a MASEM study on the net positive effect of AI use on critical thinking
articles.license_context: Publisher open access. The notes paraphrase the article.
articles.method: The authors pooled correlations from 31 studies involving 16,357 participants. Their model estimated how AI use related to critical thinking through two reported experiences, learning motivation and dependence on AI.
articles.results: The estimated indirect associations ran in opposite directions. The motivation pathway was +0.217 and the dependence pathway was −0.212. Their sum was close to zero (reported estimate 0.004, p = .645). The adjusted direct association between use and critical thinking was positive (0.149).
articles.discussion: Two people who use AI frequently can differ in why they return to it. The authors suggest examining whether it sustains interest in the work or becomes a default source of answers.
articles.limitations: Most included studies measured people at a single point in time. The model cannot establish which experience came first.

digest.idea: Two pathways behind frequent AI use
digest.explain: The analysis separates learning motivation from dependence on an AI tool.
digest.approach: The authors combined correlations from 31 studies involving 16,357 people. They asked how motivation to learn and reliance on AI each related to critical thinking.
digest.finding: AI use was linked to stronger critical thinking through motivation and to weaker critical thinking through dependence. These two estimates were nearly equal in size.
digest.interpretation: Frequency alone says little about how a learner engages.
digest.limitation: Most studies took measurements only once. They cannot tell us whether using AI changed motivation or whether already motivated learners used AI more.

articles.title: Utilizing a GPT-based exam assistant to support practice and assessment in higher education: an exploratory study on learner engagement and perceptions
articles.license_context: Publisher open access. The notes paraphrase the article.
articles.method: Thirty business undergraduates at a German university practiced organizational behavior with a GPT tutor. It asked four questions and then presented a case. In one example, students had to explain how they would handle conflict in a newly reorganized team. The tutor gave written feedback after each response. In the next unit, the same class studied human resources with instructor-written Moodle quizzes, including an exercise on calculating wages. The researchers examined practice records and surveyed students after each unit.
articles.results: The first question appeared in 224 chatbot sessions. Students typed an answer in 118 sessions (52.7%). The final case appeared in 146 sessions and drew an answer in 91 (40.6% of all launches). Students could practice repeatedly, so these counts describe sessions. Most survey respondents reported 30 minutes to two hours of weekly practice with either tool. Among the 23 who took the second survey, over half preferred the chatbot for practice or considered either format suitable. Most preferred Moodle for graded work.
articles.discussion: A teacher looking only at the 224 launches would count opening the exercise and working through the case in exactly the same way. The written answers let the authors distinguish those actions. They suggest that students may have returned to rehearse the kind of question they expected on the exam. The logs cannot show how much students learned from reading the tutor’s feedback.
articles.limitations: All students used the chatbot first and Moodle second. The subject changed between units, and the chatbot exam was supervised while the Moodle exam was taken at home. Moodle recorded 181 practice attempts without showing which questions students actually answered. The researchers could compare reported practice time, but could not tell which tool produced more active practice or better learning.

digest.idea: What happened after students opened the exam tutor?
digest.explain: A German business class practiced for one unit with a GPT tutor and the next with Moodle quizzes. The chatbot’s logs show how often an open question drew a written answer.
digest.approach: Thirty students practiced organizational behavior with a GPT tutor that gave written feedback on four questions and a case. In the next unit, they used Moodle quizzes to study human resources.
digest.finding: Of 224 chatbot sessions, 118 included an answer to the first question. The final case appeared 146 times and drew 91 answers, or 40.6% of all launches.
digest.interpretation: Counting launches alone misses the difference between seeing a question and attempting an answer. A student could start several sessions.
digest.limitation: Moodle logged 181 attempts but did not show which questions students answered. Topic, order and exam setting also differed, so the class cannot tell us which tool helped students learn more.

articles.title: Beyond the Pyramid: Bloom’s Taxonomy Meets Generative AI
articles.license_context: Publisher open access. The notes paraphrase the article.
articles.method: Austin, Gulya and Kassorla use a hypothetical biochemistry lab to ask what students must know to evaluate an AI answer. Small groups inspect an AI-generated plan for measuring an enzyme reaction and its accompanying image. They look for assumptions about temperature and other experimental conditions. A student who has studied the reaction might spot a missing control immediately. Another might need to look it up before deciding which part of the plan to change.
articles.discussion: The authors suggest letting students move repeatedly between evaluation, background reading and revision. The reasons a student gives for retaining or changing an AI suggestion become material for assessment.
articles.limitations: The authors use the class to illustrate their framework. They report no classroom observations or comparison of learning outcomes.

digest.idea: What can a student do with an answer already on the page?
digest.explain: Starting with an AI explanation changes the task a teacher can assign.
digest.approach: In a proposed biochemistry lab, students inspect an AI-generated experiment and image. They look for a missing control or an assumption about temperature and explain how they would check it.
digest.interpretation: A student’s reason for changing the procedure shows an instructor which experimental conditions they understand.
digest.limitation: The authors designed this classroom example to illustrate their framework. They have yet to test how students use it or what they learn.

articles.title: The epistemic limits of generative AI disclosure in scholarly authorship
articles.license_context: Publisher open access. The notes paraphrase the article.
articles.method: Matsui draws on journal policies and earlier studies of disclosure to develop a theory of how readers allocate attention when an author reports using AI. The paper distinguishes scrutiny that addresses a research decision from scrutiny prompted by an AI label alone. If AI contributed to an analysis, checking the code is relevant. If a writer reports grammar correction, hunting for familiar AI phrasing could draw attention away from the evidence.
articles.discussion: Matsui proposes giving readers identical manuscripts with different descriptions of editing. Reading time, comments and comprehension could help distinguish a change in where readers look from a change in how much they trust the author.
articles.limitations: The article proposes this experiment. It reports no reader-attention data.

digest.idea: Where does an AI disclosure direct a reader’s attention?
digest.explain: Matsui asks which parts of a manuscript receive extra scrutiny.
digest.approach: Matsui considers two disclosures a reader might encounter. AI-assisted analysis gives a reason to inspect the code. A note about grammar editing might instead prompt a hunt for telltale phrases.
digest.interpretation: Matsui proposes giving readers identical manuscripts with different editing disclosures and comparing what they flag and what they remember.
digest.limitation: The paper proposes a way to measure a shift in attention. It does not report how readers actually responded to either disclosure.

articles.title: Performance without capability: generative AI and the validity of assessment in higher education
articles.license_context: Publisher open access. The notes paraphrase the article.
articles.method: Kearney develops a framework for interpreting AI-assisted assignments and applies it to a hypothetical 2,000-word case analysis. It asks who made the important decisions and what evidence of those decisions an instructor can inspect. In one version, a student submits every exchange but accepts each AI suggestion unquestioningly. In another, the student weighs competing interpretations but submits only the final answer. Both leave the instructor with difficulties in judging capability, for different reasons.
articles.discussion: Kearney suggests asking students to annotate their responses to objections or orally defend two interpretive choices. Either can expose the reasoning behind a case analysis. The relevant evidence depends on the capability the assignment is intended to certify.
articles.limitations: The examples illustrate possible designs. Their effects on learning, later transfer and grading workload need empirical tests.

digest.idea: Which decision does the grade certify?
digest.explain: An essay and its chat log capture different parts of a student's work.
digest.approach: Kearney compares four hypothetical submissions for a 2,000-word case analysis. In one, a complete chat log shows a student accepting every AI suggestion. In another, only the final reasoning is visible.
digest.interpretation: Having students defend two choices orally could show which judgments they can explain themselves.
digest.limitation: The worked examples leave open how much these changes help teachers judge understanding and how much marking time they require.

articles.title: Generative artificial intelligence dependence and academic performance: serial mediation through attentional control and physical fitness and moderation by grade level
articles.method: Researchers linked questionnaires from 1,461 students aged 12–17 at urban Chinese schools to fitness tests and standardized scores in Chinese, mathematics and English. The questionnaires measured reliance on generative AI and students' reported ability to direct their attention.
articles.results: Students who reported greater dependence on AI also reported poorer attentional control and had lower academic scores. Statistical models linked dependence to scores through attentional control and fitness, separately and in combination.
articles.discussion: The survey connects students' accounts of attention to an outcome the schools recorded independently. Students already struggling to concentrate or to keep up with schoolwork might also seek more assistance.
articles.limitations: The measures came from one period. Students rated their own attention. The study did not track when they sought AI help or control for family socioeconomic circumstances.

digest.idea: How do students describe their attention when they rely on AI?
digest.explain: Teenagers' answers were linked with school records and fitness tests.
digest.approach: Researchers linked 1,461 Chinese adolescents’ ratings of AI dependence and attention to their fitness tests and their scores in Chinese, mathematics and English.
digest.finding: Students reporting greater dependence also reported more trouble directing their attention and earned lower school exam scores.
digest.interpretation: The data leave open whether struggling students turn more often to AI.
digest.limitation: The measurements came from one period. Students rated their own attention, so the study cannot establish whether concentration problems preceded their reliance on AI.

articles.title: A study on the relationships among perceived cognitive offloading, cognitive load allocation, and academic engagement in AI-empowered curriculum environments
articles.method: Jia surveyed 1,050 university students with experience using generative AI. They reported tasks delegated to it, their mental effort and their engagement with coursework. The analysis accounted for task categories, including fact retrieval and outlining.
articles.results: Reported delegation had no clear overall linear relationship with engagement. The model linked offloading with lower engagement through extraneous demands such as checking answers, and with higher engagement through effort spent understanding the material. Differences between memory-related and analytical offloading were statistically inconclusive.
articles.discussion: A student can spend time checking a generated explanation or use it to connect ideas. Separating those activities can help explain why the reported amount of delegation says little about engagement.
articles.limitations: All measures were self-reports collected at one time. The study included neither a memory test nor observations of what learners verified.

digest.idea: What work remains after a student delegates a task?
digest.explain: Checking AI output and integrating an idea can both require effort.
digest.approach: Jia asked 1,050 university students what they delegated to AI and how much effort they spent checking outputs or understanding material. Tasks included looking up facts and making outlines.
digest.finding: How much work students said they delegated did not clearly predict engagement. The model linked the burden of checking outputs with lower engagement and effort spent understanding ideas with higher engagement.
digest.interpretation: The type of mental work deserves closer measurement.
digest.limitation: Students described their effort in a one-time survey. The researchers did not observe them checking answers or test what they could recall.
